chapters.title: Prologue
paragraphs: Suppliants of all ages are seated around the altar at the palace doors, with a PRIEST OF ZEUS at their head. OEDIPUS enters to them.

OEDIPUS. My children, the youngest descendants of ancient Cadmus, why do you sit here as suppliants, holding in your hands olive branches wreathed with wool? Why is the whole city filled with the smell of incense, and echoing everywhere with lamentations and prayers? Children, I did not think it right to learn of this from others, so I have come here myself, I, Oedipus, your world-renowned king. You there — old man — whose venerable white hair marks you as the spokesman of this gathering, tell me your mood and your purpose. Is it dread of some evil that moves you, or do you come asking a favor? You cannot doubt my zeal on your behalf; I would be ruthless and hard-hearted indeed if I turned away petitioners such as you.

PRIEST. Yes, Oedipus, my sovereign lord and king, you can see for yourself how both extremes of age crowd the altars at your palace — young children barely fledged, and old men bent with years; priests, as I am of Zeus, and these, the flower of our youth. Meanwhile the common people, carrying wreathed branches, throng our two market squares, or gather before the twin shrines of Pallas, or where Ismenus gives his oracles by fire. For, as you yourself see, our ship of state, battered by storms, can no longer lift her head — she is foundering beneath a surging tide of blood. A blight has struck the ears of our corn, a blight has struck our grazing flocks and herds, a blight has struck our women in childbirth; and over all this, armed with his blazing torch, the God of Plague has swooped down on our city, emptying the house of Cadmus, while the dark kingdom of Pluto is glutted with groans and tears. That is why, O King, we sit here at your hearth, I and these children — not because we think you a new god, but because we believe you first among men; first in the ordinary misfortunes of life, and first in what the gods send down on us. Are you not the one who came to the town of Cadmus and freed us from the tribute we paid to that cruel songstress? You had no prompting from us, nor any lesson from others; no, it was by a god's inspiration (so all men believe, and bear witness) that you restored our lives. And now, O Oedipus, our peerless king, all of us, your worshippers, beg you to find some remedy — whether through a voice whispered from heaven, or through what a man's wit can discover. Tried counselors, I think, are best equipped to suggest what will come of the future. Lift up our state, O first of men, lift it up! Watch over your good name, for because of your past devotion our country hails you, justly, as its savior. Never let this be said of your reign: 'He raised us up only to cast us down.' Lift us up, build our city on a rock. Your lucky star ascending brought us good fortune once — oh, do not let it set now! If you wish to rule this land, as you now reign, it is surely better to rule a peopled kingdom than an empty one. Neither walls nor ships are worth anything if the men inside them fail.

OEDIPUS. My poor children — I know well, all too well, the mission that brings you here and what you need. I am aware that you are all sick, and yet, however great your pain, mine is greater still. Your sorrow touches each of you alone, him and no other; but I grieve at once for the city, for myself, and for you. So you have not roused a sluggard from his daydreams. Many are the tears I have shed, my children, and many are the tangled paths of thought I have wandered. Weighing all this, I found one thread of hope and followed it up: I have sent Menoeceus' son, Creon, my wife's brother, to consult Pythian Phoebus at his Delphic shrine, to learn how I might save the state by deed or word. And now, counting up the days since he set out, I wonder at his delay. It is strange, this endless tarrying, strange indeed. But when he arrives, I would be vile indeed if I failed to do everything the god commands.
PRIEST. Your words are well timed; even as you speak, that shouting tells me Creon is drawing near.
OEDIPUS. O King Apollo! May his cheerful look be the promise of cheerful news!
PRIEST. I think the news is welcome; otherwise his head would scarcely be crowned with berry-laden bay leaves.
OEDIPUS. We shall soon know; he is now within earshot.
[Enter CREON]
My royal cousin, tell me, son of Menoeceus, what message have you brought us from the god?
CREON. Good news; for even unbearable troubles, if rightly resolved, lead to nothing but good.
OEDIPUS. But how runs the oracle? So far your words give me no ground for confidence or fear.
CREON. If you wish to hear my message in public, I will tell you here and now — or else come inside with me.
OEDIPUS. Speak before them all; the burden I carry is more for my subjects than for myself.
CREON. Then let me report all the god declared. King Phoebus strictly commands us to root out a foul pollution that infests this land, and no longer to harbor an evil we have let take hold.
OEDIPUS. What kind of purification does he mean? What is wrong?
CREON. Banishment — or the shedding of blood for blood. This stain of blood is wrecking our state.
OEDIPUS. Whom can he mean? Who is the criminal he denounces?
CREON. Before you took the helm of the state, the ruler of this land was Laius.
OEDIPUS. So I have heard, but I never saw the man.
CREON. He was killed; and now the god's command is clear: punish his murderers, whoever they are.
OEDIPUS. But where are they? Where in the wide world can we find the faint, faded traces of a crime so long past?
CREON. In this land, said the god; 'whoever seeks will find; whoever sits with folded hands or sleeps is blind.'
OEDIPUS. Was he in his palace, or in the fields, or traveling, when Laius met his end?
CREON. He was abroad; he had set out, so he told us, for Delphi, but he never came back.
OEDIPUS. Did no word come, no fellow traveler who could give us some clue to follow up?
CREON. Only one man escaped, and fleeing for his life, he could tell us little of what he saw — only one thing for certain.
OEDIPUS. And what was that? One clue might take us far, if even a spark of hope can guide our search.
CREON. Robbers, he told us — not a single bandit, but a whole band of them — attacked and murdered him.
OEDIPUS. Would any bandit have dared so bold a stroke, unless he was paid off by someone here in Thebes?
CREON. So it was suspected; but in the troubles that followed, no one came forward to avenge his murder.
OEDIPUS. What trouble could have kept a full investigation from going forward, when royalty had fallen so wretchedly?
CREON. The riddling Sphinx compelled us to let the dim past slide and attend to what was right in front of us.

OEDIPUS. Well, I will start the search again and bring dark things to light. It is right that Phoebus, and you as well, should care so much for the dead; and I too, as is fitting, will lend my aid to avenge this wrong done to Thebes and to the god. This is not for some distant relative but for myself — I will drive this poison out of the blood. For whoever killed that king might well have a mind to strike me down with the same assassin's hand. So in avenging him, I serve myself. Up, children, hurry, leave these altar steps, take your suppliant branches away, and summon the people of Thebes. With the god's help, success is certain; if we fail, it is ruin.
[Exeunt OEDIPUS and CREON]
PRIEST. Come, children, let us go; these gracious words have anticipated the very purpose we came to ask. And may the god who sent this oracle save us as well, and rid us of this pestilence.
[Exeunt PRIEST and SUPPLIANTS]

chapters.title: Parodos
paragraphs: CHORUS. Sweet-voiced daughter of Zeus, from your gold-paved Pythian shrine borne to holy Thebes — what news do you bring? My soul is racked and shivers with fear. (Healer of Delos, hear us!) Do you bring some pain unknown before, or, with the circling of the years, do you call us to renew some penance from of old? Child of golden Hope, immortal voice, O tell me.

First on Athena I call — O goddess, daughter of Zeus, defend us! Goddess and sister, stand by us, Artemis, Lady of Thebes, high-throned in the heart of our marketplace! And you, Lord of the death-winged arrow! I beg for your threefold aid to save our city from death and ruin. If in days gone by, when we were on the brink of perishing, you drove the fiery plague out of our land, come near us now and defend us again!

Ah, how countless are my sorrows! Our whole people are in decline; my spirit lies unarmed. The earth denies us her kind fruits; women cry out in barren labor; life after life is struck down, swifter than the flight of a bird on the wind, swifter than the onrush of the Fire-God, to the western shores of Night.

Wasted like this by death on death, our whole city is perishing. Corpses spread infection all around; there is no one left to tend them or mourn them. On the altar steps, wives and grandmothers wail, tearing the air with long-drawn moans and piercing cries, mingled with prayers and litanies. Golden child of Zeus, O hear us — let your gracious face appear!

And grant that Ares, whose hot breath I feel, even though he stalks without shield or sword, and whose voice is the battle-shout, may turn in sudden flight, driven either to the harborless waters of Thrace or to Amphitrite's bed. For what night leaves undone, the morrow's sun strikes down and destroys. Father Zeus, whose hand wields the lightning-brand, with your bold thunderbolt we pray — slay him, O slay him!

O that your arrows too, Lycean King, might fly abroad from the taut gold bowstring, champions of our cause; yes, and the flashing torches of Artemis, with which the huntress sweeps across the Lycian steeps! You too I call, god with hair bound in gold, whose name our land carries — Bacchus, to whom your Maenads cry Evoe; come with your bright torch, rout him, O joyful god whom we adore, the god whom the gods abhor.

chapters.title: First Episode
paragraphs: [Enter OEDIPUS.]

OEDIPUS. You pray; that is well. But if you are willing to listen to my words, and to heed them, and to apply the remedy, you may perhaps find relief and comfort. Mind you, I speak as one who comes as a stranger both to the report of this murder and to the crime itself. How, unaided, could I track it far without a clue? And since I lack one (for too late was I enrolled as a citizen of Thebes), I make this proclamation to all of you: Thebans, if any of you knows the man who killed Laius, son of Labdacus, I summon him to make a clean confession to me. If he shrinks from it, let him consider this — by confessing he will escape the capital charge; the worst penalty he will suffer is banishment, and he will leave unharmed. But if any of you knows the murderer to be a foreigner from another land, let him who knows speak out, and I will see him rewarded, with my thanks besides. But if you still keep silent — if out of fear for yourselves or your friends you disregard my command — hear then what I resolve. I lay my curse upon the assassin, whoever he may be. Let no man in this land, where I hold the sovereign rule, harbor him or speak to him; let no one give him any share in prayer or sacrifice or purifying rites, but hound him out of your homes. For he is our defilement, as the god has lately shown me by oracle. So as their champion, I maintain the cause of both the god and the murdered king. And on the murderer I lay this curse — on him and on all who share his guilt — may the wretch pine away in utter wretchedness! And for myself, if with my knowledge he should be received at my own hearth, I pray that the curse I laid on others fall upon me. See that you carry out all I have commanded, for my sake and the god's sake, and for the sake of this land, a desert blasted by the wrath of heaven. For even setting aside the god's express command, it would be a scandal if you left unpurged the murder of a great man and your king, and failed to track it home. Now that I am lord, successor to his throne, his bed, his wife (and had he not been frustrated in the hope of offspring, children born of one womb would have forged a closer bond between him and me — but Fate swooped down on him) — for these reasons I, as his blood-avenger, will maintain his cause as though he were my own father, and will leave no stone unturned to track down the assassin, to avenge the son of Labdacus, son of Polydorus, of Cadmus, and of Agenor, first of the race. And for the disobedient I pray: may the gods send them no harvest from their fields, no children from their women, but may they waste and pine away, as they are wasting now, yes, and worse stricken. But to all of you, my loyal subjects who approve what I do, may Justice, our ally, and all the gods be gracious and attend you forever.

CHORUS. My king, I take the oath you propose and swear it. I did not kill him myself, nor can I name the slayer. As for the search, it would be best, I think, if Phoebus, who set the riddle, gave the answer himself — who the murderer was.
OEDIPUS. Well argued; but no living man can hope to force the gods to speak against their will.
CHORUS. May I then say what seems next best to me?
OEDIPUS. Yes, and if there is a third best, tell me that too.
CHORUS. My lord, if any man sees eye to eye with lord Phoebus, it is our prophet Teiresias; he above all could guide a searcher in this matter to the light.
OEDIPUS. Here too my zeal has not slackened. At Creon's urging I have twice sent to fetch him, and for some time I have been wondering why he is not here.
CHORUS. I remember some rumors from long ago — mere gossip.
OEDIPUS. Tell them to me; I want to know everything.
CHORUS. It was said he was killed by travelers.
OEDIPUS. So I heard, but no one has seen the man who saw him fall.
CHORUS. Well, if he knows what fear is, he will flinch and flee from the terror of your curse.
OEDIPUS. Words do not frighten a man who does not flinch at deeds.
CHORUS. But here is one to accuse him. Look, at last they are bringing in the god-inspired seer, the one man above all others in whom truth is inborn.
[Enter TEIRESIAS, led by a boy.]

OEDIPUS. Teiresias, seer who understands all things — the lore of the wise, hidden mysteries, the high things of heaven and the low things of the earth — you know, though your blinded eyes see nothing, what plague is infecting our city. We turn to you, O seer, as our one defense and shield. The messengers will surely have told you what answer the god returned when we consulted his oracle — how only one course could rid us of this plague: to find the murderers of Laius, and either kill them or drive them out of the land. So, without begrudging us either augury or any other form of divination at your command, save yourself, save your country, save your king; save us all from this defilement of bloodshed. We depend on you. This is man's highest calling — to lend all his powers to the service of others.
TEIRESIAS. Alas, alas, what misery it is to be wise when wisdom profits nothing! This old lesson I had forgotten; otherwise I would not be here.
OEDIPUS. What troubles you? Why this melancholy mood?
TEIRESIAS. Let me go home. Do not stop me. It would be best for you to bear your burden, and me to bear mine.
OEDIPUS. For shame! No true-born patriot of Thebes would hold back a word of prophecy like this.
TEIRESIAS. Your own words, O king, miss the mark; and I, for fear of stumbling the same way...
OEDIPUS. Oh, speak! Do not hold back, I beg you — if you know anything, share what you know. We are all your suppliants.
TEIRESIAS. Yes, because you are all without understanding; but my voice will never reveal my miseries — or yours.
OEDIPUS. What is this? You know something, and yet you refuse to speak? Would you betray us and destroy the state?
TEIRESIAS. I will not trouble myself, nor you. Why do you press me uselessly for what you will never hear from me?
OEDIPUS. Monster! Your silence would kindle fire out of a flint. Will nothing loosen your tongue? Can nothing move you, nothing shake your stubborn silence?
TEIRESIAS. You blame my mood, yet do not see your own — the mood you are married to; instead, you fault me.
OEDIPUS. And who could hold back his anger, hearing how insolently you scorn the state?
TEIRESIAS. What will come will come, even if I stay silent.
OEDIPUS. Since it must come, it is your duty to tell me.
TEIRESIAS. I have nothing more to say. Rage as you please, and give your pent-up anger free rein.

OEDIPUS. Yes, I am angry, and I will not spare my words — I will speak my whole mind. You, I think, are the man who planned the crime, yes, and carried it out too, all except the actual killing; and if you had not been blind, I would swear you alone committed the bloody deed.
TEIRESIAS. Is that so? Then I charge you to abide by your own proclamation. From this day, do not speak to these men, or to me. You are the man. You are the accursed polluter of this land.
OEDIPUS. Vile slanderer! You blurt out these insults, and think, I suppose, that as a seer you'll go unpunished.
TEIRESIAS. Yes, I am free — strong in the strength of truth.
OEDIPUS. Who was your teacher? Not your art, I think.
TEIRESIAS. You were — goading me against my will into speaking.
OEDIPUS. What speech? Say it again, and settle my doubt.
TEIRESIAS. Did you miss my meaning? Or are you goading me on?
OEDIPUS. I only half caught your meaning; say it again.
TEIRESIAS. I say that you are the murderer of the man whose murderer you are hunting.
OEDIPUS. You will regret it, repeating such a gross slander twice.
TEIRESIAS. Must I say more, to make your fury worse?
OEDIPUS. Say whatever you wish; it will only be wasted breath.
TEIRESIAS. I say that you are living with your closest kin in shame, and you do not know the infamy you are in.
OEDIPUS. Do you think you will always wag your tongue unscathed?
TEIRESIAS. Yes — if the power of truth counts for anything.
OEDIPUS. With other men, but not with you — for in ear, in wit, in eye, in everything, you are blind.
TEIRESIAS. Poor fool, to hurl insults at me that all these men here will soon hurl back at you.
OEDIPUS. Child of endless Night, you have no power over me or over any man who sees the sun.
TEIRESIAS. No — for it is not your fate to fall by my hand. I leave to Apollo what belongs to the god.
OEDIPUS. Is this a plot of Creon's, or your own?
TEIRESIAS. Not Creon; you yourself are your own ruin.

OEDIPUS. O wealth, and sovereign power, and skill by skill outmatched in the battlefield of life — what spite and envy follow in your wake! Look: for this crown which the state conferred on me — a gift I never sought — for this crown, the trusty Creon, my loyal friend, has been lying in wait to push me out, and has suborned this mountebank, this juggling charlatan, this tricksy beggar-priest, who is keen-eyed only for profit but stone-blind in his own art. Tell me, you — have you ever proven yourself a prophet? When the riddling Sphinx was here, why did you offer no deliverance to these people? And yet the riddle was not one to be solved by guesswork; it required the prophet's art — and in that art you were found wanting. Neither birds nor signs from heaven helped you then; but I came, simple Oedipus, and I shut her mouth by native wit, untaught by any auguries. This is the man you would now undermine, hoping to rule alongside Creon in my place. I think that you and your accomplice will soon regret your plot to drive the scapegoat out. Thank your grey hairs that you still have to learn what punishment such arrogance deserves.
CHORUS. To us it seems that both the seer and you, O Oedipus, have spoken in anger. This is no time to quarrel, but to consult how best we may fulfill the oracle.

TEIRESIAS. King though you are, free speech at least is my right — in this we are equals. I own no lord but Loxias; him I serve, and I will never be counted one of Creon's men. This then is my answer: since you have not spared to taunt me with my blindness — you have eyes, and yet you do not see into what misery you have fallen, nor where you live, nor with whom you share your bed. Do you know your lineage? No, you do not, and unwittingly you are a double enemy to your own kin, both the living and the dead. The hounding curse of mother and father, one day, shall drive you like a two-edged sword beyond our borders, and the eyes that now see clearly shall from then on know only endless night. Where will your bitter cry not reach, what crag on all Cithaeron will not echo your wailing, when you have found out on what wedding night you were brought home — carried on the gale, but to no fair harbor! Yes, and a flood of evils that you do not yet guess will set you and your children in one line. Insult Creon then, and insult my words; no mortal shall be struck down worse than you.
OEDIPUS. Must I endure this man's insolence? A plague on you! Get out! Be gone, away with you, and never cross my threshold again.
TEIRESIAS. I would never have come had you not summoned me.
OEDIPUS. I did not know you would babble nonsense — otherwise you would have waited a long time for my summons.
TEIRESIAS. Such I am — a fool in your eyes, perhaps, but wise in the eyes of the parents who bore you.
OEDIPUS. What are you saying — 'parents'? Who bore me? Speak.
TEIRESIAS. This day shall be your birthday — and your grave.
OEDIPUS. You love to speak in riddles and dark words.
TEIRESIAS. And who is as skilled as you at reading riddles?
OEDIPUS. Taunt me with the very thing my greatness rests on.
TEIRESIAS. And yet this very greatness has proven your ruin.
OEDIPUS. No matter, if I saved the commonwealth.
TEIRESIAS. Time for me to go. Come, boy, take me home.
OEDIPUS. Yes, take him away quickly — his presence vexes me and holds me up; once he is gone, he can plague me no more.

TEIRESIAS. I am going, but first I will tell you why I came. I do not fear your scowl, for you cannot harm me. Hear this: the man you have been trying to arrest all this while with threats and warrants, the wretch who murdered Laius — that man is here. He passes for a foreigner in this land, but soon he will prove to be a Theban, native-born. And yet his fortune will bring him little joy: blind instead of seeing, clad in a beggar's rags in place of royal purple, leaning on a staff, he will soon grope his way to a foreign country. And of the children within his home, he will be shown to be both brother and father — of the woman who bore him, son and husband both, bedfellow, and killer of his own father. Go inside and think about this, and if you find I have missed the mark, then declare from this day on that I have no wit or skill in prophecy.
[Exeunt TEIRESIAS and OEDIPUS]

chapters.title: First Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. Who is he — named by the immortal voice from Pythia's rocky cell — the doer of foul deeds of bloodshed, of horrors no tongue can tell? He needs a foot for flight swifter than the storm-swift steeds, for on his heels comes pursuit — armed with the lightning of his Sire, Apollo. And like sleuth-hounds, the Fates pursue.

Yes — but now the summons has flashed out from Parnassus' snowy peak: 'Seek far and near for the undiscovered doer of this murder!' Now like a sullen bull he wanders through forest thickets and upland groves, and tries in vain to flee the doom that flits always over his head, driven on still by avenging Phoebus — that divine voice from the central shrine of Earth. I am sorely troubled by the master seer's words. Are they true, are they false? I do not know, and hold my tongue for fear, fluttered by vague suspicion. Neither the present nor the future is clear. I know of no quarrel, ancient or recent, between the house of Labdacus and our ruler, the son of Polybus. There is no proof: how then can I challenge our king's good name? How can I join in a blood-feud for a crime that cannot be traced?

All-wise are Zeus and Apollo, and nothing is hidden from their sight; they are gods. And in wit one man may surpass another among mortals. But that a mortal seer knows more than I do — where has that ever been proved? Or how, without a sure sign, can I blame the man who saved our state when the winged songstress came — a man tested and tried in the sight of us all, like gold assayed? How can I now agree that a crime should be laid on Oedipus?

CREON. Friends, countrymen, I learn that King Oedipus has brought a most grievous charge against me, and I have come to protest before you. If he believes that I have harmed or injured him in any way, by word or deed, in this present trouble of ours, I do not care to prolong my life carrying that bad name; for this slander does not hit some single blemish — it ruins my good name altogether, if by the common voice I am denounced as a traitor to the state and false to you, my friends.
CHORUS. This taunt, very likely, was blurted out in temper, not said deliberately.
CREON. Did anyone dare claim that it was I who prompted the seer to utter a trumped-up charge?
CHORUS. Such things were said; with what intent I do not know.
CREON. Were his wits and his eyes not wandering astray when he fastened this monstrous charge on me?
CHORUS. I do not know; to my sovereign's actions I am blind. But look — here he comes now to answer for himself.

chapters.title: Second Episode
paragraphs: [Enter OEDIPUS.]

OEDIPUS. You there — what are you doing here? Do you have the nerve to come to my doors, you brazen-faced rogue, my would-be murderer, the filcher of my crown? Come, answer me this: did you detect in me some touch of cowardice or weak-mindedness, that you dared undertake this plot? Was I too simple, apparently, to see the serpent stealing up on me in the dark — or too weak to crush it once I saw? But it is you who are the fool, trying to seize a crown without followers or friends — a prize that only followers and wealth can win.
CREON. Listen to me. You have had your say; it is my turn to reply. Then, when you have heard me, judge.
OEDIPUS. You are glib of tongue, but I am slow to learn from you; I know your venomous hatred too well.
CREON. First I would argue this very point out with you.
OEDIPUS. Oh, do not argue that you are not a rogue.
CREON. If you count stubbornness a virtue, untaught by reason, you are much astray.
OEDIPUS. If you think a kinsman can be wronged and no punishment follow, you are much mistaken.
CREON. In that you judge rightly; but this wrong you allege — tell me what it is.
OEDIPUS. Did you, or did you not, urge me to send for the priest?
CREON. Yes, and I stand by that advice.
OEDIPUS. Tell me, how long has it been since Laius...
CREON. Since Laius...? I do not follow your drift.
OEDIPUS. ...was carried off by violent hands.
CREON. In the dim past, many years ago.
OEDIPUS. Was this same prophet practicing his craft back then?
CREON. Yes — as skilled as he is now, and no less respected.
OEDIPUS. Did he at that time ever mention me?
CREON. Not to my knowledge — never when I was present.
OEDIPUS. But was no search, no investigation, carried out?
CREON. A full inquiry was made, certainly, but nothing was learned.
OEDIPUS. Why did the seer fail to tell his story then?
CREON. I do not know, and not knowing, I hold my tongue.
OEDIPUS. This much you do know, and can surely tell me.
CREON. What do you mean? All that I know, I will declare.
OEDIPUS. If you had not put him up to it, the seer would never have charged me with the death of Laius.
CREON. Whether he did or not, you know best; but now I would put a question to you, in my turn.
OEDIPUS. Question me, and prove me a murderer — if you can.
CREON. Then let me ask you: did you marry my sister?
OEDIPUS. A fact too plain for me to deny.
CREON. And as your consort and queen, does she share the throne?
OEDIPUS. I grant her freely whatever her heart desires.
CREON. And with the two of you, do I share an equal third part of the rule?
OEDIPUS. Yes — and that is what proves you a false friend.

CREON. Not so, if you would reason with yourself as I reason with myself. First, consider: would any mortal choose a troubled reign, full of terrors, over secure peace of mind, if the same power were guaranteed to him either way? As for me, I have no natural craving for the name of king; I prefer to do kingly deeds, and every sober-minded man thinks the same. At present, all my needs are satisfied through you, and I have nothing to fear; but if I were king, my actions would often run counter to my own will. How then could a title have more appeal for me than the sweetness of boundless influence? I am not so besotted as to grasp at the shadow when I already hold the substance. As things stand, every man wishes me well; every petitioner seeks to gain my ear, if he hopes to win any favor from you. Why should I abandon the better choice for the worse? That would be pure madness, and I am not mad. Such ambition has never tempted me, nor would I ever take part in such a plot. If you doubt me, go first to Delphi and check for yourself whether my report of the god's answer was true; then investigate whether I plotted or conspired with the seer, and if it proves so, sentence me to death — not by your voice alone, but by mine together with yours. But do not condemn me out of hand, without appeal, on mere suspicion. It is not right to rate bad men good at random, or good men bad. I would as soon see a man throw away the thing he counts most precious, his own life, as see him spurn a true friend. In time you will learn the truth, for only time can reveal the just; but a villain is exposed in a day.
CHORUS. To one who walks cautiously, his words commend themselves; hasty counsels are not safe ones.
OEDIPUS. When a stealthy plotter strides in swiftly, I must be quick too with my counter-plot. To wait passively for his attack means sure success for him and certain defeat for me.
CREON. What then is your will? To banish me from the land?
OEDIPUS. I would not have you banished — no, I want you dead, so that men may see what wages envy earns.
CREON. I see you will not yield, nor believe me.
OEDIPUS. [No one but a fool would believe a man like you.]
CREON. You are not wise.
OEDIPUS. Wise for my own sake, at least.
CREON. Why not for mine too?
OEDIPUS. Why, for such a knave?
CREON. Suppose you have no sense.
OEDIPUS. Even so, kings must rule.
CREON. Not if they rule badly.
OEDIPUS. O my Thebans, hear him!
CREON. Your Thebans? Am I not a Theban too?
CHORUS. Stop, my princes — look, here, and none too soon, comes Jocasta from the palace. Who is better fitted than she to settle your quarrel?
[Enter JOCASTA.]

JOCASTA. Misguided princes, why have you stirred up this war of words? Are you not ashamed — while the whole country lies stricken — to be airing your private injuries like this? Go inside, my lord; go home, my brother; do not make a public scandal out of a petty grievance.
CREON. My royal sister, Oedipus your husband has given me a choice (O terrible alternative!) — between the exile of an outlaw and the death of a felon.
OEDIPUS. Yes, my lady; I have caught him practicing his vile arts against my royal person.
CREON. May I have no success, but die accursed, if I am guilty of this charge in any way whatsoever.
JOCASTA. Believe him, I beg you, Oedipus — for the sake of his solemn oath first, then for my sake, and for the sake of the elders who stand here waiting on you.
CHORUS. Listen, king; reflect, we beg you. Do not be stubborn — relent.
OEDIPUS. Tell me, to what should I agree?
CHORUS. Respect a man whose honesty and loyalty are known to all, and are now confirmed by oath.
OEDIPUS. Do you know what favor you are asking?
CHORUS. Yes, I know.
OEDIPUS. Then declare it, and make your meaning plain.
CHORUS. Do not brand a friend whom wagging tongues assail; do not let suspicion prevail against his sworn oath.
OEDIPUS. Are you aware that in asking this, you are in truth asking for my own death or banishment?

CHORUS. No, by the leader of the host divine! Witness, Sun above, such a thought was never mine. Unblessed, friendless, may I perish, if ever I cherished such a wish! But my heart is desolate, brooding on our stricken state — we shall fall doubly, if discord grows between the two of you, to crown all our other troubles.
OEDIPUS. Well, let him go — no matter what it costs me, whether certain death or shameful banishment. For your sake I relent, not his; and wherever he may go, my heart will still loathe him.
CREON. You are as sullen in yielding as you were truculent in your anger. Such tempers rightly plague themselves the most.
OEDIPUS. Leave me in peace and be gone.
CREON. I go — misjudged by you, but justified in the eyes of these men.
[Exeunt CREON]

chapters.title: Second Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. My lady, lead your husband inside; why linger out here any longer?
JOCASTA. First tell me how the quarrel broke out.
CHORUS. Rumors bred unjust suspicions, and injustice rankles deep.
JOCASTA. Were they both at fault?
CHORUS. Both.
JOCASTA. What was the story?
CHORUS. Ask me no more. The land is sorely distressed; better to leave sleeping troubles at rest.
OEDIPUS. Strange counsel, friend! I know you mean me well — and yet you would soften and blunt my zeal.

CHORUS. King, I say it once again: witless I would be, yes, insane, if I lightly cast aside you, my country's prop and stay — the pilot who, in her moment of danger, brought our distracted state to a quiet haven. And now — who else but you can guide us?

chapters.title: Third Episode
paragraphs: JOCASTA. Let me too, I beg you, know, O king — what is the cause that has stirred up this unrelenting anger?
OEDIPUS. I will tell you, for you are more to me than any of them. Lady, the cause is Creon and his plots.
JOCASTA. But what provoked the quarrel? Make this clear.
OEDIPUS. He points me out as Laius' murderer.
JOCASTA. From his own knowledge, or on someone else's report?
OEDIPUS. He is too cunning to commit himself to the charge, and makes a mouthpiece of a knavish seer.

JOCASTA. Then you can set your conscience at rest on that score. Listen, and I will convince you that no mortal has any share in the art of prophecy. Here is the proof, in brief. An oracle once came to Laius (I will not say it was from the Delphic god himself, but from his ministers) declaring that he was fated to die by the hand of his own son — a child that would be born to him by me. Now Laius — so the report at least affirms — was killed one day by robbers, foreigners not from this country, at a place where three roads meet. As for the child, it was only three days old when Laius, after piercing and pinning its ankles together, gave it to others to be cast away on a trackless mountainside. So Apollo did not, in the end, bring it to pass that the child should be his father's murderer, nor was the dreaded terror fulfilled with Laius being slain by his own son. Such was the seer's horoscope. O king, pay it no heed. Whatever the god thinks fit to search out, he will himself, unaided, reveal.
OEDIPUS. What memories, what wild tumult of soul came over me, lady, as I heard you speak!
JOCASTA. What do you mean? What has shocked and startled you so?
OEDIPUS. I thought I heard you say that Laius was killed at the meeting of three roads.
JOCASTA. So the story ran — and still does.
OEDIPUS. Where did this happen? Do you know the place?
JOCASTA. The land is called Phocis; the spot is where the side roads from Delphi and from Daulis meet.
OEDIPUS. And how long is it since these things happened?
JOCASTA. It was only a short while before you were proclaimed our country's ruler that the news was brought.
OEDIPUS. O Zeus, what have you willed to do with me!
JOCASTA. What is it, Oedipus, that moves you so?
OEDIPUS. Do not ask me yet; tell me the build and height of Laius. Was he still in the prime of manhood?
JOCASTA. He was tall, and his hair was lightly strewn with silver; and not unlike you in form.
OEDIPUS. O woe is me! I think I unwittingly laid a dread curse upon myself just now.
JOCASTA. What do you say? When I look at you, my king, I tremble.
OEDIPUS. A dreadful foreboding tells me that in the end the seer will prove not to be blind. One more question will settle my doubt.
JOCASTA. I am afraid; but ask, and I will answer everything.
OEDIPUS. Did he have only a few attendants, or a train of armed retainers, such as befits a prince?
JOCASTA. There were five in all, and one of them a herald; Laius rode in a mule-drawn carriage.
OEDIPUS. Alas! It is clear as noonday now. But tell me, lady — who carried this report back to Thebes?
JOCASTA. A serf, the sole survivor who returned.
OEDIPUS. Is he perhaps close at hand, or in the house?

JOCASTA. No. As soon as he came back and found you reigning in the place of the slain Laius, he clasped my hand and begged me to send him to the high pastures in the mountains, where he would be farthest from the sight of Thebes. And so I sent him. He was an honest slave and deserved some better reward.
OEDIPUS. Fetch him at once. I have a strong desire to see the man.
JOCASTA. He shall be brought; but why do you summon him?
OEDIPUS. Lady, I fear my tongue has run past discretion; that is why I would question him.
JOCASTA. Very well, he shall come. But may I not too have a share in the burden on your heart, my king?

OEDIPUS. You shall not be denied your wish. My imaginings have gone this far already. Who has a higher claim than you to hear my tale of dire adventures? Listen, then. My father was Polybus of Corinth, and my mother Merope, a Dorian; and I was counted the foremost citizen there, until a strange thing happened to me — strange indeed, yet scarcely deserving all the heat it stirred up. At a banquet a reveler, flushed with wine, shouted that I was not the true son of my father. It vexed me, but for the moment I swallowed the insult; on the next day I went to my mother and father and questioned them. They were indignant at the random slur cast on my parentage and did their best to comfort me; but still the poisoned barb rankled, for the scandal kept spreading and growing. So, in secret and without their leave, I went to Delphi; and Apollo sent me away cheated of the knowledge I had come to seek. Yet other grievous things he did prophesy — woes, laments, mourning, dread omens: that I was to defile my mother's bed, and raise up children too loathsome to look upon, and slay the father from whose loins I sprang. Then, lady — now you shall hear the very truth — as I drew near that triple branching of the roads, a herald met me, and a man seated in a chariot drawn by colts — just as in your story. The man in front and the old man himself tried to thrust me roughly off the path. Then, jostled in anger by the charioteer, I struck him, and the old man, seeing this, waited till I was passing and from his car brought a two-pronged goad down full on my head. But I paid him back with interest — one stroke of my good staff was enough to fling him clean out of his seat and lay him flat on his back. And so I killed them, every one. But if between that stranger and Laius there was anything in common, who could be more miserable than I, what mortal could you find more loathed by the gods? A wretch whom no stranger, no citizen, may shelter or even speak to, whom all are bound to drive out of their homes. And this very curse I laid upon myself, and laid it by no other hand. Yes, with these bloodstained hands I pollute the bed of the man I killed. Tell me — am I not vile? Am I not utterly unclean, a wretch doomed to exile, and in exile forbidden the sight of all my dearest ones, never to walk my native earth again? Or else to marry my own mother, and slay my father Polybus, who begot me and raised me? If someone were to say that this is the handiwork of some inhuman power, who could fault their judgment? But — you pure and awful gods, forbid, forbid that I should ever see that day! May I be blotted out from among the living before such a mark of pollution is branded on me!
CHORUS. We too, O king, are troubled; but until you have questioned the survivor, keep hoping.
OEDIPUS. My hope is faint, but enough of it survives to make me wait for this herdsman to come.
JOCASTA. Suppose him here — what would you learn from him?
OEDIPUS. I will tell you, lady: if his tale agrees with yours, I shall have escaped calamity.
JOCASTA. And what of special importance did I say?

OEDIPUS. In your report of what the herdsman said, Laius was killed by robbers — plural. Now if he still speaks of robbers, not a single robber, then I did not kill him; 'one' cannot square with 'many.' But if he says a lone wayfarer did it, the last link in the chain of my guilt is forged.

JOCASTA. Well, rest assured — his tale ran that way from the start, and he cannot now retract what he said then. Not only I, but all our townspeople heard it. Even if he changes his story somewhat now, he cannot make the death of Laius square in any way with the oracle. For Loxias said plainly he was doomed to die by my child's hand; yet that poor babe shed no blood, but perished first himself. So much for divination! From now on, I will look for signs neither to right nor left.
OEDIPUS. You reason well. Still, I would have you send and fetch the bondsman here. See to it.
JOCASTA. I will, at once. Come, let us go inside. I would do nothing that my lord dislikes.
[Exeunt OEDIPUS and JOCASTA]

chapters.title: Third Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. May my lot be still to lead a life of innocence, and to flee irreverence in word or deed — to follow still those laws ordained on high, whose birthplace is the bright ethereal sky. No mortal birth they claim; Olympus alone is their progenitor. Never shall they slumber in cold oblivion; the god in them is strong, and does not grow old.

Of insolence is the tyrant bred; insolence full blown, glutted with empty riches, scales the precipitous height and grasps the throne. Then topples over, and lies in ruin, flat on the ground — no foothold on that dizzy steep. But may Heaven keep the true patriot, who burns with eager zeal to serve the state. God is my help and my hope; on him I wait.

But the proud sinner — in word or in deed — who will not heed Justice, who will not reverence the shrines of the divine images: let perdition seize his vain imaginings, if, urged on by profane greed, he grasps at ill-gotten gain, and lays an impious hand on the holiest things. Who, when such deeds are done, can hope to escape heaven's thunderbolts? If sin like this can rise to honor, why do I still dance and lead the sacred choir?

I will go no more to earth's central oracle, nor to Abae's hallowed cell, nor bring my votive offering to Olympia — if God's truth is not made plain before all men. O Zeus, reveal your might; king, if that is your true name, omnipotent, all-seeing, as of old. For Laius is forgotten; his fate — men pay no heed to it; Apollo is abandoned, and faith grows cold.
[Enter JOCASTA.]

JOCASTA. My lords, you look amazed to see your queen with garlands and gifts of incense in her hands. I had a mind to visit the high shrines, for Oedipus is overwrought, alarmed with manifold terrors. He will not use his past experience, as a man of sense would, to judge the present; he lends an ear to any croaker who augurs ill. Since my own counsel avails nothing, I turn to you, our present help in time of trouble — Apollo, Lord of the Wolf's land — and here I bring my prayers and supplications to you. Lighten us, lord, and cleanse us of this curse! For now we are all cowed, like sailors who see their helmsman struck dumb in the storm.
[Enter Corinthian MESSENGER.]
MESSENGER. My masters, tell me where the palace of Oedipus is — or better still, where is the king?
CHORUS. Here is the palace, and he is within; this is his queen, the mother of his children.
MESSENGER. May all happiness attend her and her household; blessed is her husband, and her marriage bed.
JOCASTA. My greetings to you, stranger; your fair words deserve a like response. But tell me why you have come — what is your business, what is your news?
MESSENGER. Good news for your husband and for the royal house.
JOCASTA. What news might that be? Whose messenger are you?
MESSENGER. The people of the Isthmus have resolved to make your husband king — so it was being reported there.
JOCASTA. What! Is not aged Polybus still king?
MESSENGER. No, truly; he is dead and in his grave.
JOCASTA. What! Is he dead — the father of Oedipus?
MESSENGER. If I speak falsely, may I die myself.

JOCASTA. Quick, girl, carry this news to my lord. You god-sent oracles, where do you stand now! This is the man whom Oedipus long shunned, in dread of proving to be his murderer; and now he dies in the course of nature, not by his hand.

chapters.title: Fourth Episode
paragraphs: [Enter OEDIPUS.]
OEDIPUS. My wife, my queen, Jocasta, why have you summoned me from the palace?
JOCASTA. Hear this man, and as you hear him, judge what has become of all those awe-inspiring oracles.
OEDIPUS. Who is this man, and what is his news for me?
JOCASTA. He comes from Corinth, and his message is this: your father Polybus has passed away.
OEDIPUS. What? Let me hear it, stranger, from your own mouth.
MESSENGER. If I must first make my message clear beyond doubt — know that Polybus is dead.
OEDIPUS. By treachery, or did sickness strike him?
MESSENGER. One small touch sends an old man to his rest.
OEDIPUS. So he died of some illness, poor man.
MESSENGER. Yes, after he had measured out the full span of his years.

OEDIPUS. To think of it, my lady! Why then should anyone take any notice of the Pythian hearth, or of the birds shrieking in the air? Did they not point me out as doomed to kill my father? Yet he is dead and in his grave, and here am I who never unsheathed a sword against him — unless his longing for his absent son killed him, in which case I slew him in a sense. But as they stand, the oracles are dead — dust, ashes, nothing — as dead as Polybus.
JOCASTA. Tell me, did I not foretell this long ago?
OEDIPUS. You did — but I was misled by my fear.
JOCASTA. Then let this weigh no longer on your soul.
OEDIPUS. Must I not still fear my mother's marriage bed?

JOCASTA. Why should a mortal man, the sport of chance, with no sure foreknowledge, be afraid? Best to live a carefree life from day to day. As for this marriage with your mother — do not be afraid. How often a man has in his dreams slept with his mother! The man who least regards such feverish phantasies lives most at ease.
OEDIPUS. I should share your confidence in full, if my mother were not living; but since she lives, though half convinced, I must still live in dread.
JOCASTA. And yet your father's death lights up the darkness considerably.
OEDIPUS. Considerably, yes — but my fear is about her who is still alive.
MESSENGER. Who may this woman be whom you so fear?
OEDIPUS. Merope, stranger, the wife of Polybus.
MESSENGER. And what about her could cause you any fear?
OEDIPUS. A heaven-sent oracle, of dreadful meaning.
MESSENGER. Is it a mystery — or may a stranger hear it?

OEDIPUS. No, it is no secret. Loxias once foretold that I would sleep with my own mother, and with my own hands shed the blood of my own father. That is why, for many a year, Corinth has been a home kept distant from me; and I have roamed abroad, but have missed the sweetest sight of all — my parents' faces.
MESSENGER. Was this the fear that drove you into exile from home?
OEDIPUS. Yes — and the dread of killing my own father.
MESSENGER. Why then, King, since I have come to bring you joy, have I not rid you of this second fear as well?
OEDIPUS. Well, you shall have a fitting reward for your trouble.
MESSENGER. Well, I confess that what chiefly made me come was the hope of some profit from your coming home.
OEDIPUS. No — I will never again go near my parents.
MESSENGER. My son, it is plain you do not know what you are doing.
OEDIPUS. How so, old man? For heaven's sake, tell me everything.
MESSENGER. If this is why you dread returning home.
OEDIPUS. Yes — so that the god's word is not fulfilled in me.
MESSENGER. For fear that through your parents you would be accursed?
OEDIPUS. That and nothing else is my constant dread.
MESSENGER. Do you not know that your fears are entirely baseless?
OEDIPUS. How baseless, if I am truly their son?
MESSENGER. Because Polybus was nothing to you by blood.
OEDIPUS. What are you saying? Was Polybus not my father?
MESSENGER. As much your father as I am — no more, no less.
OEDIPUS. My father no more to me than a complete stranger?
MESSENGER. Since I did not beget you, nor did he.
OEDIPUS. What reason had he, then, to call me his son?
MESSENGER. Know this — he took you from my hands, as a gift.
OEDIPUS. And yet, though I was no child of his, he loved me dearly.
MESSENGER. A childless man till then, he took you to his heart.
OEDIPUS. A foundling — or a bought slave — this child he took?
MESSENGER. I found you in the wooded glens of Cithaeron.
OEDIPUS. What brought you up to wander those upland glades?
MESSENGER. My job was to tend the flocks on the mountain.
OEDIPUS. A vagrant shepherd, hired out for wages?
MESSENGER. True — but your savior in that hour, my son.
OEDIPUS. My savior? From what harm? What was wrong with me then?
MESSENGER. Those ankle joints are evidence enough.
OEDIPUS. Ah, why remind me of that ancient wound?
MESSENGER. I loosed the pin that riveted your feet together.
OEDIPUS. Yes — from my cradle I have carried that dreadful brand.
MESSENGER. And from that came the name you still bear.
OEDIPUS. Who did it? I beg you, tell me — who? Was it my father, my mother?
MESSENGER. I do not know. The man from whom I got you may know more.
OEDIPUS. What — another man found me, not you yourself?
MESSENGER. Not I; another shepherd gave you to me.
OEDIPUS. Who was he? Would you know him again if you saw him?
MESSENGER. He passed, as they say, for one of Laius' household.
OEDIPUS. The king who ruled this country long ago?
MESSENGER. The same: he was a herdsman of the king.
OEDIPUS. And is he still living, so that I may see him?
MESSENGER. His fellow countrymen would know that best.
OEDIPUS. Does any bystander here know the herdsman he speaks of — either from seeing him in the fields or in the city? Answer straight! The hour has come to clear this business up.
CHORUS. I think he means none other than the herdsman whom you were just now eager to see; but our queen Jocasta could tell you best.
OEDIPUS. Madam, do you know the man we sent to fetch? Is he the same of whom the stranger speaks?
JOCASTA. Who is the man? What does it matter? Let it go. It is a waste of thought to weigh such idle words.
OEDIPUS. No — with clues like these to guide me, I cannot fail to bring the secret of my birth to light.
JOCASTA. Oh, as you care for your life, give up this search. The anguish I endure is enough.
OEDIPUS. Take heart. Even if I am proved the son of a bondwoman — yes, a slave three descents over — your honor is unspotted.
JOCASTA. Yet humor me, I beg you; do not do this.
OEDIPUS. I cannot; I must probe this matter to the bottom.
JOCASTA. It is for your own sake that I advise you for the best.
OEDIPUS. I grow impatient with this 'best advice' of yours.
JOCASTA. Ah, may you never discover who you are!
OEDIPUS. Go, fetch me the herdsman here, and leave this woman to glory in her proud ancestry.
JOCASTA. O woe is you, poor wretch! With that last word I leave you, silent from now on, forever.
[Exit JOCASTA]
CHORUS. Why, Oedipus — why has the queen, stung with such passionate grief, rushed away like that? I much fear that out of this dead calm a storm of woes will burst.

OEDIPUS. Let the storm burst; my resolve is fixed — I will learn my lineage, however low it be. Perhaps she, with all a woman's pride, scorns my base parentage. But I, who count myself the favorite child of Fortune, the giver of good gifts, shall not be shamed. Fortune is my mother, and the changing moons my brothers, and with them I wax and wane. Sprung from such stock, why should I fear to trace my birth? Nothing can make me other than I am.

CHORUS. If my soul's prophecy does not err, if my wisdom is worth anything, then, Cithaeron, I shall hail you, before tomorrow's full moon rises, as the nurse and foster-mother of our Oedipus, and shall exalt you as is fitting. Dance and song shall sing your praises, lover of our royal race. Phoebus, may my words find favor!

Child, who bore you? Some nymph, some goddess? Surely your father was more than mortal — perhaps the hill-roaming Pan. Or did Loxias beget you, who haunts the upland wolds? Or the lord of Cyllene, or Bacchus, dweller on the cold hilltops? Did some Oread of Helicon give you to him, a newborn joy — one of the nymphs with whom he loves to sport?

OEDIPUS. Elders, though I have never met the man before, if I may make a guess — I think I see the herdsman we have long been seeking. His worn old look matches the years of the aged messenger there; besides, I seem to recognize the men who are bringing him as servants of my own. But you, perhaps, having in past days known or seen the herdsman, may be better able than I to confirm my guess.
CHORUS. I recognize him; one of Laius' household — a simple herdsman, but as trustworthy as any man.
[Enter HERDSMAN.]
OEDIPUS. Corinthian stranger, I address you first. Is this the man you mean?
MESSENGER. This is he.
OEDIPUS. And now, old man, look up and answer everything I ask. Were you once of Laius' household?
HERDSMAN. I was — a slave, not purchased, but born into the house.
OEDIPUS. What was your business? How were you employed?
HERDSMAN. For the best part of my life I tended sheep.
OEDIPUS. What were the pastures you most frequented?
HERDSMAN. Cithaeron and the neighboring mountains.
OEDIPUS. Then you must have known this man there — at least by reputation?
HERDSMAN. This man? In what way? What man do you mean?
OEDIPUS. The man here — having met him in times past...
HERDSMAN. Offhand, I cannot call him well to mind.

MESSENGER. No wonder, master. But I will revive his faded memories. I am sure he can recall the time when we pastured our flocks together on the slopes of Cithaeron — he with two, I with one — for three long summers; I was his fellow from spring till Arcturus rose; then when winter came, I drove mine home, and he drove his to the folds of Laius. Did these things happen as I say, or not?
HERDSMAN. It was long ago, but all that you say is true.
MESSENGER. Well, then, you must remember giving me a child to rear as my own foster son?
HERDSMAN. Why do you ask me this? What of it?
MESSENGER. Friend, the man standing before you was that child.
HERDSMAN. A plague on you! Hold that reckless tongue of yours!
OEDIPUS. Softly, old man, do not rebuke him. Your words deserve punishment more than his.
HERDSMAN. Best of masters, what is my offense?
OEDIPUS. Not answering his question about the child.
HERDSMAN. He speaks at random, babbling like a fool.
OEDIPUS. If you will not speak of your own accord, I will loosen your tongue.
HERDSMAN. For mercy's sake, do not abuse an old man.
OEDIPUS. Arrest the villain — seize him and tie his hands!
HERDSMAN. Alas, alas! What have I done? What more do you want to know?
OEDIPUS. Did you give this man the child he is asking about?
HERDSMAN. I did — and would to god I had died that day!
OEDIPUS. And die you shall, unless you tell the truth.
HERDSMAN. But if I tell it, I am doubly ruined.
OEDIPUS. The scoundrel, I see, still means to dodge and weave.
HERDSMAN. No — I have already confessed I gave him the child long ago.
OEDIPUS. Where did it come from? Was it yours, or given to you?
HERDSMAN. I had it from another; it was not my own.
OEDIPUS. From which of our townsmen? From what house?
HERDSMAN. For god's sake, master, hold back — ask no more.
OEDIPUS. If I have to question you again, you are done for.
HERDSMAN. Well then — it was a child of Laius' house.
OEDIPUS. Slave-born, or of Laius' own bloodline?
HERDSMAN. Ah me — I stand on the perilous edge of speech.
OEDIPUS. And I on the edge of hearing — but still I must hear it.
HERDSMAN. Know then, the child was reputed to be his own; but she within, your wife, could tell you best.
OEDIPUS. What! She — she gave it to you?
HERDSMAN. It is so, my king.
OEDIPUS. With what intent?
HERDSMAN. To make away with it.
OEDIPUS. What — she, its own mother?
HERDSMAN. Fearing a dreadful prophecy.
OEDIPUS. What prophecy?
HERDSMAN. It was foretold that he would kill his own father.
OEDIPUS. Why then did you give it to this old man?

HERDSMAN. Out of pity, master, for the baby. I thought he would take it to the country he came from; but he saved it for the worst of miseries. For if you are truly what this man says, God pity you — you were born to misery.

OEDIPUS. Ah me, ah me! All has come to pass, all is true! O light, may I look on you no more! I stand a wretch, cursed in my birth, cursed in my marriage, a parricide, a man of incest — thrice cursed!
[Exit OEDIPUS]

chapters.title: Fourth Stasimon
paragraphs: CHORUS. Races of mortal men, whose life is but a span — I count you but the shadow of a shade! For he who seems to know the most of happiness holds only its semblance; a moment, and the vision pales and fades. Your fall, O Oedipus, your pitiable fall warns me to call no one born of woman blessed.

For he, O Zeus, outshot the best of marksmen and won the highest prize of wealth and power. By him the vulture-maid was beaten down, her witchery laid to rest; he rose as our savior and the land's strong tower. We hailed you king, and from that day on, you were adored as the absolute lord of mighty Thebes.

O heavy hand of fate! Who is now more desolate, whose tale more sorrowful than yours, whose lot more dire? O Oedipus, uncrowned head — your cradle became your marriage-bed; one harborage sufficed for son and sire. How could the soil your father plowed so long endure, in silence, to bear such a wrong?

All-seeing Time has caught out Guilt, and brought to justice son and sire commingled in one bed. O child of Laius' ill-starred race, I wish I had never looked upon your face — for you I raise a lament as for the dead. And yet, in truth, through you I drew new breath; and now through you I feel a second death.

chapters.title: Exodos
paragraphs: [Enter SECOND MESSENGER.]

SECOND MESSENGER. Most grave and reverend senators of Thebes, what deeds you must soon hear, what sights you must soon behold — how you will mourn, if, true-born patriots, you still reverence the race of Labdacus! Not the Ister, nor all the flood of Phasis, could wash away the bloodstains from this house — the evils it conceals, or will soon bring to light — evils wrought not unwittingly, but with intent. The hardest to bear are the wounds we inflict on ourselves.
CHORUS. Grievous enough, our past calamities, for all our tears and groans. What more can you add?
SECOND MESSENGER. My story is quickly told and quickly heard. Our sovereign lady, queen Jocasta, is dead.
CHORUS. Alas, poor queen! How did she come to her death?

SECOND MESSENGER. By her own hand. All the horror of it — since you did not see it — you cannot take in. Even so, as far as my poor memory serves, I will tell you the unhappy lady's suffering. When, in her frenzy, she had passed through the entrance-hall, she rushed straight for the bridal chamber, clutching at her hair with both her hands; and once inside the room, she slammed the doors shut behind her with a crash. 'Laius!' she cried, and called upon the name of the husband long, long dead; her mind was on the son she had borne him — the son by whom the father was murdered and the mother left to breed with her own seed, a monstrous progeny. Then she wailed over the marriage bed on which, poor wretch, she had conceived a double brood — husband by husband, children by her own child. What happened after that, I cannot tell, nor how the end came about, for with a shriek Oedipus burst in upon us; all eyes were fixed on Oedipus as he strode up and down, and we could not mark her agony to the end. For pacing to and fro, he cried 'A sword! Where is the wife who is no wife — the teeming womb that bore a double harvest, me and mine?' And in his frenzy, some supernal power (no mortal, surely, none of us who watched him) guided his footsteps. With a terrible shriek, as though someone were beckoning him on, he crashed against the folding doors, wrenched the bolts from their staples, and hurled himself inside. Then we beheld the woman, hanging there, a running noose twisted round her neck. But when he saw her, with a maddened roar he loosed the cord; and when her wretched corpse lay stretched on the ground, what followed — O, it was dreadful! He tore the golden brooches that held up her queenly robes, raised them high, and struck full on his own eyeballs, uttering words like these: 'No more shall you behold such sights of misery — deeds I have suffered and deeds I have done; from this day on, quenched in darkness, you shall see only those you should never have seen; now blind to those whom, while I could see, I longed in vain to know.' Such was the burden of his cry; and not once but many times he struck his eyes with his uplifted hand, and at each blow the bloodied eyeballs drenched his beard — not oozing drop by drop, but one dark gory downpour, thick as hail. Such are the evils that, breaking out from this double source, have overwhelmed them both, confounding man and wife. Till now the storied fortune of this house was fortunate indeed; but from this day on, woe, lamentation, ruin, death, disgrace — every ill that can be named — all, all are theirs.
CHORUS. But has he still no respite from his pain?

SECOND MESSENGER. He cries, 'Unbar the doors, and let all Thebes behold the slayer of his father, his mother's —' — that shameful word my lips cannot repeat. He vows to fly, a self-exile, from the land, and not stay to bring upon his house the curse he himself has uttered; but he has no strength, nor anyone to guide him, and his torture is more than a man can bear, as you yourselves will see. For look, the palace doors are opening, and soon you shall see a sight so sad that even the man who loathed him most would pity it.
[Enter OEDIPUS blinded.]

CHORUS. What a pitiful sight! No more pitiful have these sad eyes ever looked upon. What madness is this? Who is it that cast this spell on you, prowling all around your life, leaping upon you with a demon's bound? Hapless wretch! How can I bear to look upon your misery? Though I yearn to gaze on you, to ask many things, to learn much — horror-struck, I must turn away.
OEDIPUS. Ah me! Ah, woe is me! Where am I being carried? How like a ghost forlorn my voice flits from me through the air! On, on the demon drives me. The end — ah, where?
CHORUS. An end too dreadful to tell, too dark to see.
OEDIPUS. Dark, dark! The horror of darkness, like a shroud, wraps around me and bears me on through mist and cloud. Ah me, ah me! What spasms shoot across my body, what pangs of agonizing memory?
CHORUS. No wonder, in such a plight, that you feel the double weight of past and present woes.
OEDIPUS. Ah friend, still loyal, still constant and kind — you care for the blind. I know you are near, and though bereft of eyes, I know your voice.
CHORUS. O doer of dread deeds, how could you mar your sight like this? What demon drove you on?
OEDIPUS. Apollo, friend, Apollo — he it was who brought these evils to pass; but the right hand that struck the blow was mine, no other's. How, how could I go on seeing, when sight brought me no joy?
CHORUS. Alas! It is as you say.

OEDIPUS. Tell me, friends — can any look, or voice, or touch of love ever gladden my heart again? Hurry, friends, do not delay in love of me — take this twice-cursed man away, far from any sight, the man abhorred by the gods and accursed of men.
CHORUS. Your despair well suits your desperate case. I wish I had never looked on your face!
OEDIPUS. My curse on the man who untied the cruel fetters of the waif, and revived my life! He meant me well, and yet, had he left me there, he would have saved me and my friends a world of misery.
CHORUS. I too could wish it had been so.

OEDIPUS. Then I would never have come to shed my father's blood, nor climbed into my mother's bed; the monstrous offspring of a womb defiled, consort of the one who fathered me, and his child besides. Was ever a man afflicted like this before, like Oedipus?
CHORUS. I cannot say that you have counseled yourself well, for it would have been better for you to be dead than living and blind.

OEDIPUS. What was done was well done. You can never shake my firm conviction of that. No more arguments. For if I had still my sight, with what eyes could I have met my father in the shades, or my poor mother, since against the two of them I sinned a sin no gallows could atone for? And you say, perhaps, that the sight of one's children gladdens a parent's eye. What, born as mine were born? No, such a sight could never bring me joy; nor this fair city, with its battlements, its temples, and the statues of its gods — sights from which I, now the wretchedest of all men, once the foremost Theban in all of Thebes, am cut off by my own sentence, condemned by my own proclamation against the wretch, the criminal declared unclean by heaven itself — and of the race of Laius. Thus branded as a felon by myself, how could I have dared to look you in the face? No — had I known a way to choke off the springs of hearing too, I would not have hesitated to make a dungeon of this miserable body, cut off from sight and from sound; for it is bliss to dwell in a place sorrow cannot reach. Why did you harbor me, Cithaeron? Why did you not take me and kill me? Then I should never have shown mankind the secret of my birth. O Polybus, O Corinth, O my home — home of my ancestors, as you were called — how fair a nursling then I seemed, how foul the canker that lay festering in the bud! Now the blight stands revealed, root and fruit. You triple high-roads, and you hidden glen, copse, and pass where the three branched ways meet — you drank my blood, the lifeblood these hands spilled, my father's; do you happen to recall those deeds of mine which you witnessed, and the work I did afterwards, when I came to Thebes? O fatal wedlock — you gave me birth, and having borne me, sowed my seed again, mixing the blood of fathers, brothers, children, brides, wives and mothers — an incestuous brood — all the horrors that can be done beneath the sun, horrors too foul to name. O, I beg you, hide me somewhere far from this land, or kill me on the spot, or cast me down into the depths of the ocean, out of sight. Come here, condescend to touch an abject wretch; draw near and do not fear; I myself must bear the load of guilt that no one but I can share.
[Enter CREON.]
CREON. Look, here is Creon, the one man left to grant your prayer by action or by advice, for he is now the sole guardian of the state in your place.
OEDIPUS. Ah me! What words can I find to speak to him? What cause has he to trust me? In the past I have been shown to be his bitter enemy.

CREON. I do not come to mock you, Oedipus, nor to reproach you with your past misdeeds. (To BYSTANDERS) But shame on you — if you feel no sense of common human decency, at least reverence the Sun, whose light beholds and nurtures all. Do not leave a horror like this bare for all eyes to stare at, one which neither earth nor rain from heaven nor the light of day will endure. Lead him inside at once, for it is fitting that a kinsman's griefs be heard by kin and seen by kin alone.
OEDIPUS. O listen — since your coming to me is a shock of glad surprise, so noble are you, and I so vile — grant me one small favor. I ask it not for my own sake, but for yours.
CREON. And what is the favor you would ask of me?
OEDIPUS. Thrust me out beyond your borders as quickly as you can; set me in some vast desert where no mortal voice shall greet me again.
CREON. I would have done it already, but I thought it my duty first to consult the god.
OEDIPUS. His will was plainly declared — to destroy the parricide, the criminal; and I am he.
CREON. Yes, so he said; but in our present plight it would be better to consult the god once more.
OEDIPUS. Do you dare to inquire on behalf of such a wretch?
CREON. Yes, for now even you yourself would believe his word.

OEDIPUS. Yes, and with all humility I lay this charge upon you: let her who lies within receive such burial as you may ordain; such rites it is yours, as her brother, to perform. But for myself, O let my Thebes, the city of my fathers, never be doomed to bear the burden of my presence while I live. No — let me be a dweller on the hills, on yonder Mount Cithaeron, famed as mine, the tomb predestined for me by my father and mother, while they lived, so that I may die as they sought to kill me when alive. This much I know for certain — no disease shall end my days, nor any ordinary chance; for I would never have been snatched from death unless I was predestined for some dreadful doom. So be it. I care not how Fate deals with me. But my unhappy children — for my sons be not concerned, Creon, they are men, and wherever they may be, they can shift for themselves. But for my two daughters, poor innocent maidens, who always sat beside me at the table, sharing my food, drinking from my cup — for their sake, I beg you, care for them; and if you will, O might I feel their touch and make my lament. Hear me, O prince, my noble-hearted prince! If I could only blindly touch them with my hands, I should think they were still mine, as when I could see them.
[ANTIGONE and ISMENE are led in.]
What am I saying? Can it be my pretty ones whose sobs I hear? Has Creon pitied me and sent me my two darlings? Can this be?
CREON. It is true; it was I who procured you this delight, knowing what joy they were to you in former days.

OEDIPUS. God speed you! And as a reward for bringing them, may Providence deal with you more kindly than it has dealt with me! O my children, where are you? Let me clasp you with these hands, a brother's hands, a father's — hands that made lackluster sockets of his once bright eyes; hands of a man who blindly, recklessly, became your father by the very woman from whom he himself was born. Though I cannot see you, I must weep to think of the evil days to come, and of the slights and wrongs that men will heap on you. Wherever you go, to feast or festival, it will be no merrymaking for you; instead you will often come home in shame, in tears. And when you come of marriageable age, where is the bold suitor who will risk taking on himself such disrepute as must cling to my children's children? For what of infamy is missing here? 'Their father killed his own father, sowed the seed in the place from which he himself was bred, and begot these daughters at the source from which he sprang.' Such are the jeers that men will hurl at you. Who then will marry you? None, I think; you must pine away, poor maidens, in unwed barrenness. O Prince, son of Menoeceus, I turn to you — for you alone can be a father to them, now that we their natural parents are both lost. O do not leave them to wander poor and unwed, your own kin; do not let them share my lowly state. Pity them — so young, and but for you utterly destitute. Your hand on it, Prince. To you, my children, I had much to say, if only you were old enough to hear it. Let this be enough: pray that you may find some home and live content, and may your lot prove happier than your father's.
CREON. You have wept enough; go inside.
OEDIPUS. I must obey, though it is hard.
CREON. Do not weep; everything must have its day.
OEDIPUS. Well, I go — but on conditions.
CREON. Tell me your terms for going.
OEDIPUS. Send me from this land, an exile.
CREON. Ask that of the gods, not of me.
OEDIPUS. But I am the gods' abhorrence.
CREON. Then they will grant your plea soon enough.
OEDIPUS. Lead me away, then — I am willing.
CREON. Come; but let your children go.
OEDIPUS. Do not rob me of these, my children!
CREON. Do not crave mastery in everything, for the mastery that raised you was your ruin and brought about your fall.

CHORUS. Look, countrymen and Thebans — this is Oedipus the great, the man who knew the riddle of the Sphinx, and was mightiest in our state. Who among our townsmen did not gaze on his fame with envious eyes? Now, in what a sea of troubles he lies sunk and overwhelmed! Therefore, wait to see the ending of a life before you call any mortal blessed — wait till, free from pain and sorrow, he has reached his final rest.
